newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY DENIES SECRET DAM DEAL WITH SLOVAKIA.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY DENIES SECRET DAM DEAL WITH SLOVAKIA.

text.p: Hungary denied on Monday it was about to reach a secret out-of-court settlement with Slovakia over the controversial Gabcikovo dam project which has diverted a large stretch of the Danube.

Forty-five leading Hungarian artists, historians and opposition politicians, demanded at the weekend the release of minutes of ongoing expert talks between the two countries following accusations by opposition party Fidesz that Hungary had offered to build its own hydropower plant.

"No agreement, either secret or public has been reached or even drafted," Hungary's chief negotiator Janos Nemcsok told reporters. "The purpose of these negotiations is technical -- to find common ground for further talks."

The countries have fought over Slovakia's unilateral diversion in 1992 of a considerable part of the Danube waters for the dam project after Hungary quit a joint deal which planned a similar dam at Nagymaros in Hungary.

Slovakia claims Hungary breached its contract while the Hungarians say diverting the river, which forms the border between the two countries, breaks international law and has caused widespread ecological damage.
Both have presented their case in written form at the International Court in the Hague, which is due to consider it in March.

At the same time the two sides have opened talks at an expert level to explore a possible out-of-court settlement but Fidesz and the environment group the Danube Circle said last week any resultant deal would weaken Hungary's case by denying the chance to have the dam condemned internationally.
They also quoted unnamed Slovak sources as saying the Hungarians had offered to build a hydroelectric power station upstream from Nagymaros at Esztergom, where a new bridge is planned.
Nemcsok told reporters publication of the expert negotiations have to remain confidential while the International Court case is pending but denied the reports of the new offer.
"There has never been any discussion of a power plant at Esztergom and there are no plans to build any power plants anywhere," Nemcsok said.
He defended the exploratory talks, which he said were customary in cases before the international court.

"The Hungarian government is not obsessed by reaching an out-of-court settlement at any cost," he said. "Our major objective is to settle the issue as soon as possible in order to minimise the cost and the damage."
